claim: Salmonella is one of the most common foodborne pathogens, resulting in inflammatory gastroenteritis and frequently accompanied by dysbiosis.
source: Salmonella is one of the most common foodborne pathogens, resulting in inflammatory gastroenteritis and frequently accompanied by dysbiosis.
evidence: This is a general statement about Salmonella that draws from established scientific knowledge about this pathogen.

claim: Gut commensals, such as Lactobacillus species, have been proven to exhibit broad antibacterial activities and protect hosts against pathogenic infections.
source: Gut commensals, such as Lactobacillus species, have been proven to exhibit broad antibacterial activities and protect hosts against pathogenic infections.
evidence: This statement references established scientific knowledge about Lactobacillus species and their protective properties.

claim: Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus strain P118 was screened from 290 isolates recovered from fermented yogurts and healthy piglet intestines.
source: Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus strain P118, screened from 290 isolates recovered from fermented yogurts and healthy piglet intestines using traditional and Caenorhabditis elegans-infection screening strategies, exerts great probiotic properties.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental screening process used to identify P118.

claim: P118 and its supernatant exhibited great antibacterial activities.
source: Notably, P118 and its supernatant exhibited great antibacterial activities and attenuated C. elegans susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: P118 and its supernatant attenuated C. elegans susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
source: Notably, P118 and its supernatant exhibited great antibacterial activities and attenuated C. elegans susceptibility to Salmonella infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from C. elegans infection assays.

claim: P118 protected mice against Salmonella lethal infections by enhancing colonization resistance.
source: We found that P118 protected mice against Salmonella lethal infections by enhancing colonization resistance, reducing pathogen invasion, alleviating intestinal pro-inflammatory response, and improving microbial dysbiosis and fecal metabolite changes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from murine infection models.

claim: P118 protected mice against Salmonella lethal infections by reducing pathogen invasion.
source: We found that P118 protected mice against Salmonella lethal infections by enhancing colonization resistance, reducing pathogen invasion, alleviating intestinal pro-inflammatory response, and improving microbial dysbiosis and fecal metabolite changes.

claim: P118 protected mice against Salmonella lethal infections by improving microbial dysbiosis.

claim: P118 protected mice against Salmonella lethal infections by improving fecal metabolite changes.

evidence: This is supported by metabolomics analysis data.

claim: P118 administration significantly decreased the relative abundances of Salmonella.
source: Microbiota and fecal metabolome analyses suggested P118 administration significantly decreased the relative abundances of potentially harmful microbes (e.g., Salmonella, Anaeroplasma, Klebsiella) and increased the fecal levels of tryptophan and its derivatives (indole, indole-3-acrylic acid, 5-hydroxytryptophan, 5-methoxyindoleacetate).
evidence: This is supported by microbiota analysis data.

source: Deterministic processes determined the gut microbial community assembly of P118-pretreated mice.

claim: P118 probiotic activities in enhancing host tolerance to Salmonella infection were mediated by microbe-derived tryptophan/indole metabolites.
source: Integrated omics further demonstrated that P118 probiotic activities in enhancing host tolerance to Salmonella infection were mediated by microbe-derived tryptophan/indole metabolites (e.g., indole-3-acrylic acid, indole, tryptophan, 5-methoxyindoleacetic acid, and 5-hydroxytryptophan).
evidence: This is supported by integrated omics analysis combining microbiota and metabolomics data.

claim: Approximately 1.7 billion childhood diarrhea cases are recorded annually.
source: Approximately 1.7 billion childhood diarrhea cases are recorded annually, with diarrhea responsible for over 480,000 deaths for children aged <5 years and over 500,000 deaths for adults aged >70 years each year (Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Diarrhea is responsible for over 480,000 deaths for children aged <5 years each year.
source: Approximately 1.7 billion childhood diarrhea cases are recorded annually, with diarrhea responsible for over 480,000 deaths for children aged <5 years and over 500,000 deaths for adults aged >70 years each year (Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Diarrhea is responsible for over 500,000 deaths for adults aged >70 years each year.
source: Approximately 1.7 billion childhood diarrhea cases are recorded annually, with diarrhea responsible for over 480,000 deaths for children aged <5 years and over 500,000 deaths for adults aged >70 years each year (Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Salmonella infection leads to substantial gastroenteritis incidents.
source: As one of the most common foodborne enteric pathogens, Salmonella infection leads to substantial gastroenteritis incidents, imposing enormous economic burdens on global society and posing disproportionate threats to animal and human health (Stanaway et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Salmonella has evolved strategies to subvert colonization resistance conferred by intestinal commensals.
source: Salmonella has evolved strategies to subvert colonization resistance conferred by intestinal commensals and evade host immune defense responses, contributing to the increasing incidence of Salmonellosis (Caballero-Flores et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Salmonella has evolved strategies to evade host immune defense responses.
source: Salmonella has evolved strategies to subvert colonization resistance conferred by intestinal commensals and evade host immune defense responses, contributing to the increasing incidence of Salmonellosis (Caballero-Flores et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Salmonella-contaminated food is estimated to cause a total global economic loss of over $3.5 billion annually in the US.
source: Salmonella-contaminated food (meat, eggs, dairy) is considered the leading cause of Salmonellosis, estimated to cause a total global economic loss of over $3.5 billion annually in the US (Stanaway et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antibiotic treatment has been the primary strategy to control Salmonella infectious diseases.
source: Traditionally, antibiotic treatment has been the primary strategy to control Salmonella infectious diseases (Zhou et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The global abuse of antibiotics has raised significant concerns about antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
source: However, the global abuse of antibiotics has raised significant concerns about antimicrobial resistance (AMR), foodborne antibiotic residues, and compromises in treating antimicrobial-resistant bacterial infections (Wang et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbial dysbiosis induced by antimicrobials increases the susceptibility to pathogen infection.
source: Microbial dysbiosis induced by antimicrobials, enteric infections, and irregular dietary habits increases the susceptibility to pathogen infection and other diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease (Gillis et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gut commensal microbes and their derivatives protect the host against pathogen infections by providing colonization resistance against enteric pathogens.
source: Gut commensal microbes and their derivatives have been proven to exhibit broad antimicrobial activities and protect the host against pathogen infections by providing colonization resistance against enteric pathogens, limiting pathogen colonization, invasion, and transmission, and maintaining intestinal barrier function (Caballero-Flores et al., 2023; Jacobson et al., 2018; Yaqoob et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Probiotic species such as Lactobacillus exert beneficial effects on the host by enhancing colonization resistance and immune defense.
source: As one of the intestinal commensal microbes, probiotic species (without residues in raw food products), such as Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Bacillus, and yeast (e.g., Saccharomyces boulardii, S. cerevisiae), exert beneficial effects on the host by enhancing colonization resistance and immune defense, inhibiting colonization and invasion against pathogens, and maintaining gastrointestinal homeostasis (Han et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Traditional strategies for screening probiotic candidates are both time-consuming and labor-intensive.
source: Although many candidate probiotic isolates have been uncovered from fermented foods and mammalian intestines (Sakandar and Zhang, 2021; Wang et al., 2022), the traditional strategies for screening these candidates are both time-consuming and labor-intensive, involving bacterial isolation, culturing, phenotypic characterization, randomized controlled trials, and various in vitro and in vivo tests to assess probiotic properties (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Emerging evaluation strategies for probiotic candidates, such as whole-genome sequencing-based approaches and small invertebrate models, have gained significant attention due to their high-throughput, replicable, and standardized properties.
source: While culture-dependent methods are classic strategies, emerging evaluation strategies for candidates, such as whole-genome sequencing-based approaches and small invertebrate models (e.g., Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila), have gained significant attention due to their high-throughput, replicable, and standardized properties (Sun et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Intestinal macrophages play vital roles in maintaining gut homeostasis, regulating inflammation, and particularly in promoting the resolution of inflammation.
source: Intestinal macrophages play vital roles in maintaining gut homeostasis, regulating inflammation, and particularly in promoting the resolution of inflammation (Lavelle and Sokol, 2020; Na et al., 2019), which has been considered a novel potential target for controlling intestinal pro-inflammatory disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Probiotics-derived metabolites can mediate the beneficial effects of probiotics on the host health by interacting with the host gastrointestinal immune cells and gut residents.
source: It has been reported that probiotics-derived metabolites, such as bacteriocins, antimicrobial compounds, short-chain fatty acids, and tryptophan/indole derivatives, can mediate the beneficial effects of probiotics on the host health by interacting with the host gastrointestinal immune cells and gut residents (Britton and Faith, 2021; Sanders et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bacterial tryptophan metabolism produces indole derivatives which are potent bioactive ligands for the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR).
source: Bacterial tryptophan metabolism produces indole derivatives (e.g., indole-3-acetic acid, 3-indolepropionic acid, 3-indoleacrylic acid, indole-3-lactic acid, indole-3-aldehyde, indole-3-acetaldehyde), which are potent bioactive ligands for the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) (Agus et al., 2018; Koh and Bäckhed, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Indole derivatives play crucial roles in maintaining gut barrier integrity and homeostasis by activating AHR signaling pathway.
source: These indole derivatives play crucial roles in maintaining gut barrier integrity and homeostasis by activating AHR signaling pathway (Agus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Limosilactobacillus reuteri-produced indole derivatives have been reported to exert anti-inflammatory effects by activating AHR signaling pathway.
source: Limosilactobacillus reuteri-produced indole derivatives have been reported to exert anti-inflammatory effects by activating AHR signaling pathway (Cervantes-Barragan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A total of 290 bacterial isolates were isolated and identified from 33 fermented yogurt samples and 6 healthy piglet rectal content samples.
source: After being identified by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization-Time of Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), a total of 290 bacterial isolates were isolated and identified from 33 fermented yogurt samples and 6 healthy piglet rectal content samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the isolation and identification process.

claim: The 290 isolates consist of 63 Streptococcus isolates, 158 Lactobacillus/Lacticaseibacillus/Limosilactobacillus isolates, and 69 Enterococcus isolates.
source: Those isolates consist of 63 Streptococcus isolates, 158 Lactobacillus/Lacticaseibacillus/Limosilactobacillus isolates, and 69 Enterococcus isolates (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: 27 isolates were screened out by milk-clotting activity assay.
source: In the traditional/classic approach, 27 isolates were screened out by milk-clotting activity assay (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1), among which two isolates (P118 and P199) exhibited the highest tolerance to bile salt (0.3–2.0%) (Figure 1B) and biofilm formation capabilities (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two isolates (P118 and P199) exhibited the highest tolerance to bile salt (0.3–2.0%).
source: In the traditional/classic approach, 27 isolates were screened out by milk-clotting activity assay (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1), among which two isolates (P118 and P199) exhibited the highest tolerance to bile salt (0.3–2.0%) (Figure 1B) and biofilm formation capabilities (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: P118 and P199 exhibited the highest biofilm formation capabilities.
source: In the traditional/classic approach, 27 isolates were screened out by milk-clotting activity assay (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1), among which two isolates (P118 and P199) exhibited the highest tolerance to bile salt (0.3–2.0%) (Figure 1B) and biofilm formation capabilities (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: P118 strain exhibited the highest susceptibility to multiple antimicrobials compared with the P199 strain.
source: Compared with the P199 strain, P118 strain exhibited the highest susceptibility to multiple antimicrobials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. elegans has been widely used as an invaluable model for understanding the conserved mechanisms of host–microbe interactions due to the similarities of gut morphology and physiological function with human and animal.
source: C. elegans has been widely used as an invaluable model for understanding the conserved mechanisms of host–microbe interactions due to the similarities of gut morphology and physiological function with human and animal (Kumar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 8 out of 290 isolates significantly increased the survivals and prolonged the life span of S. Typhimurium-infected C. elegans.
source: In the C. elegans infection approach, 8 out of 290 isolates significantly increased the survivals and prolonged the life span of S. Typhimurium-infected C. elegans (p<0.05), and three isolates (P118, P119, P120)-treated worms were more resistant to S. Typhimurium infection than the other isolates (p<0.05) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three isolates (P118, P119, P120)-treated worms were more resistant to S. Typhimurium infection than the other isolates.
source: In the C. elegans infection approach, 8 out of 290 isolates significantly increased the survivals and prolonged the life span of S. Typhimurium-infected C. elegans (p<0.05), and three isolates (P118, P119, P120)-treated worms were more resistant to S. Typhimurium infection than the other isolates (p<0.05) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The fermented supernatants of P118 significantly inhibited the growth of multiple pathogens.
source: To illustrate the probiotic properties of L. rhamnosus P118, antibacterial activity evaluation in vitro was further conducted, and the results showed that the fermented supernatants of P118 significantly inhibited the growth of multiple pathogens (e.g., Salmonella, Yersinia, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Citrobacter rodentium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Riemerella anatipestifer) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: High-dose and anaerobic cultures of P118 exhibited more antibacterial effects than low-dose and aerobic cultures.
source: Interestingly, the inhibitory effect of P118 against S. Typhimurium was in dose- and oxygen-dependent manners, and results showed that high-dose and anaerobic cultures exhibited more antibacterial effects than low-dose and aerobic cultures, respectively (p<0.05) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The antibacterial activities of the fermented supernatant were sensitive to alkalinity (pH>5.0).
source: The results showed that the antibacterial activities of the fermented supernatant (pH=3.4) were sensitive to alkalinity (pH>5.0), trypsin, proteinase-K, pepsin, and high temperature (>70℃), but were resistant to catalase treatment (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The antibacterial activities of the fermented supernatant were sensitive to trypsin.
source: The results showed that the antibacterial activities of the fermented supernatant (pH=3.4) were sensitive to alkalinity (pH>5.0), trypsin, proteinase-K, pepsin, and high temperature (>70℃), but were resistant to catalase treatment (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The active secreted factors in the fermented supernatant were protein- or peptide-based active agents.
source: The results showed that the antibacterial activities of the fermented supernatant (pH=3.4) were sensitive to alkalinity (pH>5.0), trypsin, proteinase-K, pepsin, and high temperature (>70℃), but were resistant to catalase treatment (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is inferred from the sensitivity to proteases and heat, which is consistent with protein/peptide properties.

claim: The fermented cultures and supernatants of P118 significantly inhibited the growth of S. Typhimurium in vitro.
source: The fermented cultures and supernatants of P118 not only significantly inhibited the growth of S. Typhimurium in vitro (Figure 1I), but also protected worms against S. Typhimurium infection (Figure 1G, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The fermented cultures and supernatants of P118 protected worms against S. Typhimurium infection.
source: The fermented cultures and supernatants of P118 not only significantly inhibited the growth of S. Typhimurium in vitro (Figure 1I), but also protected worms against S. Typhimurium infection (Figure 1G, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Heat-treated P118 and P118 lysates exhibited no antibacterial activities in vitro.
source: Although they exhibited no antibacterial activities in vitro (Figure 1I), the protective activities of heat-treated P118 and P118 lysates against S. Typhimurium pathogenesis were observed in C. elegans but weaker than that of the fermented cultures and supernatants (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The protective activities of heat-treated P118 and P118 lysates against S. Typhimurium pathogenesis were observed in C. elegans but weaker than that of the fermented cultures and supernatants.
source: Although they exhibited no antibacterial activities in vitro (Figure 1I), the protective activities of heat-treated P118 and P118 lysates against S. Typhimurium pathogenesis were observed in C. elegans but weaker than that of the fermented cultures and supernatants (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: P118 draft genome was most closely related to L. rhamnosus subspecies (NCTC13710 and BIO5326).
source: The results showed that species-level identity for P118 isolate with 2.99 Mb genome size was confirmed at p<0.0001 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1K, Supplementary file 4), and P118 draft genome was most closely related to L. rhamnosus subspecies (NCTC13710 and BIO5326) (Figure 1K, Supplementary file 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Genomic analysis revealed the presence of putative bacteriocin synthesis genes in P118 isolate.
source: Genomic analysis using antiSMASH and BAGEL4 databases revealed the presence of putative bacteriocin synthesis genes in P118 isolate (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Putative bacteriocins predicated in P118 isolate showed high homology with known class II bacteriocins.
source: Putative bacteriocins predicated in P118 isolate showed high homology with known class II bacteriocins (IIa carnobacteriocin B2 produced by C. maltaromaticum, IIb enterocin X produced by Enterococcus faecium KU-B5, IId/b lactococcin A/G, and some novel bacteriocin-encoded hypothetical proteins).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: Administration of P118 significantly protected mice against Salmonella-induced deaths.
source: Administration of P118 significantly protected mice against Salmonella-induced deaths and body weight losses (Figure 2B and C), accompanied by the alleviated splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, shortened gastrointestinal tract, and clinical and pathological score (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Administration of P118 significantly protected mice against Salmonella-induced body weight losses.
source: Administration of P118 significantly protected mice against Salmonella-induced deaths and body weight losses (Figure 2B and C), accompanied by the alleviated splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, shortened gastrointestinal tract, and clinical and pathological score (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: P118 administration alleviated Salmonella-induced splenomegaly.
source: Administration of P118 significantly protected mice against Salmonella-induced deaths and body weight losses (Figure 2B and C), accompanied by the alleviated splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, shortened gastrointestinal tract, and clinical and pathological score (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: P118 administration alleviated Salmonella-induced hepatomegaly.
source: Administration of P118 significantly protected mice against Salmonella-induced deaths and body weight losses (Figure 2B and C), accompanied by the alleviated splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, shortened gastrointestinal tract, and clinical and pathological score (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: P118 significantly limited Salmonella colonization in the intestinal tissues (duodenum and colon).
source: Meanwhile, P118 significantly limited Salmonella colonization in the intestinal tissues (duodenum and colon) and invasion into the peripheral organs (liver and spleen) of mice, thereby markedly reducing Salmonella fecal shedding (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: P118 significantly limited Salmonella invasion into the peripheral organs (liver and spleen).
source: Meanwhile, P118 significantly limited Salmonella colonization in the intestinal tissues (duodenum and colon) and invasion into the peripheral organs (liver and spleen) of mice, thereby markedly reducing Salmonella fecal shedding (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: P118 markedly reduced Salmonella fecal shedding.
source: Meanwhile, P118 significantly limited Salmonella colonization in the intestinal tissues (duodenum and colon) and invasion into the peripheral organs (liver and spleen) of mice, thereby markedly reducing Salmonella fecal shedding (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Salmonella infection-induced ileal mucosal damage was alleviated by P118 administration.
source: Additionally, Salmonella infection-induced ileal mucosal damage was alleviated by P118 administration, as illustrated by the increased ileal villus height (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), ratio of villus height/crypt depth (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), ileal microvilli height and density (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the upregulated Tjp1 mRNA expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and the downregulated Il1b mRNA expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), accompanied by the reduced Il1b level in serum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and supplementary figures.

claim: P118 intervention significantly increased the numbers of Ki67-positive cells (proliferating cells) in the ileum.
source: Intervention with P118 significantly increased the numbers of Ki67-positive cells (proliferating cells), Muc2-positive cells (goblet cells), and decreased the numbers of F4/80-positive cells (macrophages) and F4/80+ Nos2+ cells (pro-inflammatory macrophages) in the ileum (Figure 2H) and also attenuated the pathological damages of peripheral organs (liver and spleen) caused by Salmonella infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.
